pages.title: About the firm
pages.content:
A firm paid only by you.

Hoshi Wealth Partners · Seattle, since 2009

Hoshi Wealth Partners is a fee-only firm founded in 2009 by Naomi Hoshi-Clarke. Seven people in Seattle work with about 140 households, and the only fee is the one the household pays.

A firm paid only by you

Hoshi Wealth Partners was founded in 2009 by Naomi Hoshi-Clarke and named for her. It is a fee-only firm: the household that receives the advice is the household that pays for it. There is no commission behind the recommendation, no product fee folded into a fund, and no performance fee tied to a result the firm will not promise. The office is at 1418 Western Avenue, Suite 600, Seattle, WA 98101.

About 140 households work with the seven people here. The firm stayed small on purpose. A written plan, a retirement-income question, an investment policy, or an estate conversation still sits with a named adviser, not with a queue. The first meeting is free. Everything after it is priced in dollars on the fees page, and the same prices apply in every conversation.

Why fee-only, and why small

Fee-only is the structure, not a slogan. When the firm is paid only by the client, the plan does not have to carry a product in order to be finished. Naomi Hoshi-Clarke set the firm up that way in 2009 and the partners have kept it. Tomás Ferreira writes the investment policy. Priya Raman coordinates tax and estate questions with the household's own attorney and tax preparer. Henrik Aalto works with owners who are selling or passing on a firm.

The firm does not sell investments of its own. Custody stays at an independent custodian, which the firm does not name because the custodian is not the advice. Staying near 140 households is how seven people still know the file. A larger book would need a different kind of firm. This one is not becoming that firm.

What the work actually is

The work begins with a written financial plan when a household wants one: one fee of $4,800, three meetings, a document the household keeps. Some households stay for ongoing planning at $7,200 a year, billed quarterly. Some ask the firm to manage investments, at 0.80 percent a year on the first $2 million and 0.50 percent a year above that, with a minimum of $9,600 a year. Some need a defined project at $380 an hour.

None of those prices buys a promise about markets. The approach is a written investment policy, low-cost index funds, rebalancing by rule, and a quarterly report in plain words. Two review meetings a year are part of the ongoing relationship. The policy is updated yearly. That is the whole machinery. It is meant to be readable by the people who live with it.

Founder

Chapter: 02 — Founder

A letter from the founder

Naomi Hoshi-Clarke · Founding partner

I founded Hoshi Wealth Partners in 2009 so the fee would come from the family in the room and from no one else. I still sit with three-generation families and with people who have retired or are about to. The shared house, the education fund, the pension that has to become a monthly income: those are the conversations I know. The firm is seven people. Tomás, Priya, and Henrik are partners. Grace Mwangi, Samuel Ortiz-Bell, and Lena Fischer keep the plans, the paperwork, and the compliance close to the same table.

We do not take commissions. We do not sell products. We do not charge for performance. If a household needs a specialist we do not employ, we say so and stay in our lane. You can write to me through hello@hoshiwealth.example or call +1 206 555 0148. The introductory meeting is sixty minutes, on Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday, in the Seattle office or by video, and it costs nothing.

Meet the people

HOSHI-CLARKE

What we do not do

The firm does not accept commissions.

A recommendation is not paid for by the product being recommended.

The firm does not sell proprietary products, and it does not collect product fees.

The firm does not charge performance fees.

A good year in a market is not an invoice, and a bad year is not a discount dressed up as skill.

The firm does not promise a return, a ranking, or a result.

Investing involves risk, including loss of principal, and no strategy assures a profit.

The firm does not custody assets.

Holdings sit with an independent custodian.

The firm does not advertise awards, and it does not borrow other firms' reputations.

If a request needs a lawyer, a tax preparer, or a specialist the household already trusts, that person stays the specialist.

Our coordination is with them, not instead of them.

pages.title: People
pages.content:
Seven people, one table.

Grace Mwangi and Samuel Ortiz-Bell

Seven people work at Hoshi Wealth Partners. Four partners lead the advice, and three associates carry planning, client service, and the firm's operations.

People

Chapter: 01

Partner 01

Naomi Hoshi-Clarke

Founding partner, family wealth & retirement income

Introduction

Naomi Hoshi-Clarke is founding partner. Her work is family wealth and retirement income. She serves three-generation families and retirees. She founded the firm in 2009 and it carries her name. Households who have shared a house across generations, or who are turning a working life into a monthly income, usually start with her. She led the Moreau-Adeyemi relationship from 2014, three generations around one plan, a shared house, and a grandchild's education fund.

She also works with Walter and June Brennan, two retiring teachers arranging pensions and savings into monthly income. She does not publish a personal track record. The introductory meeting she offers is the firm's: sixty minutes, no fee, no pitch, on Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday, in the Seattle office or by video.

Related

  • Retirement income
  • The Moreau-Adeyemi family
  • Walter and June Brennan
  • Introductory meeting

Partner 02

Tomás Ferreira

Partner, chief investment officer

Introduction

Tomás Ferreira is a partner and the chief investment officer. He serves the work of portfolio construction and investment policy. When a household asks the firm to manage investments, the policy is written before the holdings are chosen. Tomás is the partner who keeps that order. The policy names the mix, the low-cost index funds that carry it, and the rule for rebalancing. It is updated yearly. He does not trade stories about a quarter, and he does not offer a forecast as a service.

On the people page he is the second partner, after Naomi. Households who want to know why a holding is there, and what would make it change, are in his part of the work. The quarterly report is written so a client can read the policy back without a translator.

Related

  • Investment management
  • Approach
  • Fees
  • Letters

Partner 03

Priya Raman

Partner, tax & estate coordination

Introduction

Priya Raman is a partner. Her practice is tax and estate coordination. She serves widowed and single clients, estates, and giving. She does not replace the household's attorney or tax preparer. She reads the plan beside those documents so the investment policy, the will, and the gift are not three unrelated files. Widowed and single clients often arrive with accounts in more than one name and a calendar of decisions that used to be shared.

Priya's work is to put those decisions in an order the client can keep. Giving is part of the same conversation when a household wants a fund, a bequest, or a yearly gift written into the plan. She appears on the services row for tax and estate coordination, and the fees for planning or hourly project advice are the fees that apply.

Related

  • Tax and estate coordination
  • The Moreau-Adeyemi family
  • Written financial plan
  • Disclosures

Partner 04

Henrik Aalto

Partner, business owners

Introduction

Henrik Aalto is a partner. He works with business owners: owners selling a firm, owners passing a firm on, and owners whose pay is partly equity. The household and the company are easy to blur. Henrik's work is to keep the family's plan readable while the ownership changes. Rosa Delgado, who owns a furniture workshop and is preparing to sell it to her employees, is the story that shows the shape of this work.

The page does not describe a price for her firm or a date for the sale. Those facts belong to her, and they are not a result the firm claims. A business-owner engagement may be a written plan, ongoing planning, investment management, or hourly project advice. The fee schedule is the same schedule every other household sees.

Related

  • Rosa Delgado
  • Planning
  • Hourly project advice
  • Introductory meeting

Associates

Grace Mwangi

Associate adviser

Grace Mwangi is an associate adviser. She serves young families writing their first plans. Amir and Hana Saleh, young parents at the start of that work, are the household attached to her on the stories page. A first plan is often the first time the household has seen its accounts, its debts, and its hopes in one document. Grace prepares that document with the partners, not beside them.

The written financial plan is $4,800, three meetings, one fee. If the household later wants ongoing planning, the retainer is $7,200 a year, billed quarterly. Grace does not manage a separate book of investments and does not quote a return. Her work is the first plan, clearly written, for a family that has not had one before.

Samuel Ortiz-Bell

Client service manager

Samuel Ortiz-Bell is client service manager. He serves the paperwork, the transfers, and the meeting notes. After an introductory meeting, someone has to collect statements, open the path to the independent custodian, and write down what was decided. That is Samuel's work. He is not an adviser selling a second service. He sits with Grace on the day-to-day of the office so the partners' meetings turn into a file the household can recognise.

Transfers are to the unnamed independent custodian, not into a product of the firm, because the firm has no product. Meeting notes go back to the client in plain words. If a document is missing, he says which one. The office phone is +1 206 555 0148, and the desk email is hello@hoshiwealth.example.

Lena Fischer

Operations & compliance

Lena Fischer leads operations and compliance. She serves custody, reporting, and disclosures. The independent custodian holds the assets. Lena's work is to see that the firm's records match what the custodian reports, that the quarterly report goes out as the relationship requires, and that the disclosures a household should read are the ones on this site. She does not sit as a planning partner.

She keeps the operational promises specific: billing quarterly in arrears on the ongoing retainer, no commissions, no product fees, no performance fees. Questions about how a fee was calculated, including the investment-management schedule of 0.80 percent and 0.50 percent, can be answered from the fees page without a private formula. She is the seventh person at the table.

pages.title: Approach
pages.content:
Fewer moves, better reasons.

A report, a pen, a cup

The approach is a written investment policy, low-cost index funds, rebalancing by rule, and a quarterly report in plain words. The firm does not promise returns.

01 04

Approach

Chapter: 02

Principle 01

Written policy first

More

The investment policy is written before holdings are chosen. Tomás Ferreira, chief investment officer, treats that order as the job. The policy states what the money is for, how long it has to last, and what mix the household can live with. Only then does the firm select low-cost index funds to match the policy. A household can read the policy without a market commentary attached.

It is updated yearly, not whenever a headline feels urgent. Naomi's retirement-income clients, Henrik's owners, and Grace's first-plan families all receive the same sequence if they ask the firm to invest. The policy is a document, not a mood. If the household's life changes, the policy is rewritten in a review. It is not silently replaced by a new set of funds.

Related

  • Investment management
  • Tomás Ferreira

Principle 02

Costs we can control

More

The firm prefers low-cost index funds because the expense is one of the few figures an adviser can choose rather than hope for. Fund costs, the firm's own fee, and unnecessary trading are the costs in view. Investment management is 0.80 percent a year on the first $2 million and 0.50 percent a year above that, with a minimum of $9,600 a year. Planning fees are separate and published. The firm adds no commission and no product fee.

It does not add a performance fee when markets rise. Controlling cost is not a claim that the portfolio will outrun a market. It is a refusal to layer charges the household did not ask for. The quarterly report names the costs the household is paying. If a cheaper fund fits the same policy, the policy says so, and the change follows the rebalancing rule rather than a sales idea.

Related

  • Fees
  • Two worked examples

Principle 03

Rebalance by rule

More

Rebalancing is done by a rule written in the policy, not by a feeling about the next season. When a holding drifts from the mix the household agreed, it is brought back. When it has not drifted, it is left alone. That is the meaning of fewer moves. The firm does not treat activity as proof of care. Tomás Ferreira keeps the rule in the policy so a client can ask, at any quarterly report, whether the rule was followed.

A rule can be changed. It is changed in writing, at the yearly update or when a review shows that the household's life has changed. It is not changed because a market was loud in a given month. The same rule covers retirees drawing income and families still contributing. The purpose differs. The discipline of writing the change down does not.

Related

  • Investment management
  • Letters

Principle 04

Report in plain words

More

Every ongoing relationship receives a quarterly report in plain words. The report says what the policy is, what changed because the rule required it, and what the household paid. It is not a letter about the firm's outlook. Two review meetings a year give the household time to question the report with the adviser who signed the work. Naomi, Tomás, Priya, Henrik, or Grace may lead that meeting, depending on the plan.

Samuel Ortiz-Bell keeps the notes. Lena Fischer sees that the report and the custodian's records can be read together. Plain words are a standard, not a tone. If a sentence only makes sense to the person who wrote it, it is rewritten before it is sent. The household should be able to explain its own policy to a spouse, a child, or a trustee.

Related

  • Introductory meeting
  • Letters

What we will not promise

The firm will not promise a return. It will not publish a performance number and ask a household to infer a future one. It will not say that a strategy assures a profit. Investing involves risk, including loss of principal. Past markets are not a forecast, and this site does not recite them. The firm will not promise that a plan removes tax, that an estate coordination prevents dispute, or that a business sale completes on a date.

Priya coordinates with the household's tax preparer and attorney. Henrik plans beside an owner. Neither signs the other profession's work. The firm will not promise that being fee-only makes the advice correct. Fee-only describes who pays. Judgment still has to be explained, in the policy and in the quarterly report, where the household can see it.

pages.title: Services
pages.content:
Plans that outlast a market.

A first plan at the living-room table

The firm offers planning, retirement income, investment management, and tax and estate coordination. Each service is fee-only, priced in dollars, and tied to a named adviser.

Services

Chapter: 03

Service 01

Planning

Naomi Hoshi-Clarke · Grace Mwangi

More

A written financial plan is the firm's one-off planning service. The fee is $4,800 and includes three meetings. The household keeps the document. Planning is for people who want a first map or a full reset: young parents such as Amir and Hana Saleh, working with Grace Mwangi, or a three-generation family such as the Moreau-Adeyemi household, clients since 2014, working with Naomi Hoshi-Clarke. The plan can stand alone. It does not require investment management.

If the household later wants ongoing planning, the retainer is $7,200 a year, billed quarterly in arrears. Hourly project advice at $380 an hour is there when the question is narrower than a full plan. The plan states what the money is for. It does not state what the market will do. Fees and the four family stories are linked from this service because the price and the kind of household should be visible together.

Related

  • Fees
  • Amir and Hana Saleh
  • The Moreau-Adeyemi family
  • Introductory meeting

Service 02

Retirement income

Naomi Hoshi-Clarke

More

Retirement income is the work of turning pensions and savings into a monthly income a household can live on. Naomi Hoshi-Clarke leads it. Walter and June Brennan, two retiring teachers, are the story that shows the shape: pensions and savings arranged as income, with no claim about how large the income became. The work may be a written plan, the ongoing retainer, or investment management if the household asks the firm to hold the policy. Withdrawals are written into the investment policy so the mix and the spending are not invented separately each year.

The policy is updated yearly. A quarterly report shows whether the rule was followed. The firm does not promise that a retirement income will last a stated number of years beyond what the plan itself calculates for that household, and it does not publish sample incomes. The introductory meeting is the place to learn whether this service is the right one.

Related

  • Walter and June Brennan
  • Fees
  • People

Service 03

Investment management

Tomás Ferreira

More

Investment management puts the written policy into low-cost index funds and rebalances by the rule in that policy. Tomás Ferreira, chief investment officer, is responsible for portfolio construction. The fee is 0.80 percent a year on the first $2 million and 0.50 percent a year above $2 million, with a minimum of $9,600 a year. A household with $1.5 million invested pays $12,000 a year. A household with $3 million pays $16,000 plus $5,000, which is $21,000 a year.

Those are fee illustrations, not projections of account growth. Custody is at an independent custodian. The firm does not earn a commission or a product fee on the funds. Reports arrive quarterly. Two review meetings a year are included in the ongoing relationship. The firm will manage money only after the policy is written. It will not manage money against a promised return.

Related

  • Approach
  • Fees
  • Letters

Service 04

Tax and estate coordination

Priya Raman

More

Tax and estate coordination is Priya Raman's work with widowed and single clients, with estates, and with giving. She also sits with families whose plan includes a bequest or a yearly gift, including households like the Moreau-Adeyemi family, where three generations and an education fund share one table. Coordination means the plan, the investment policy, and the household's estate documents are read together. It does not mean the firm prepares the tax return or drafts the will.

Those remain with the tax preparer and the attorney the household chooses. The service is billed as a written plan, as part of the ongoing retainer, or as hourly project advice at $380 an hour, depending on the scope. The firm does not take a share of a gift, an estate, or a charitable transfer. There is no product attached to the coordination.

Related

  • The Moreau-Adeyemi family
  • Hourly project advice
  • Disclosures

pages.title: Fees
pages.content:
Plain fees, in dollars.

A report face-down, a pen, a cup

Fees are published in dollars: a free introductory meeting, a written plan, a yearly planning retainer, investment management in two bands, and an hourly rate.

The six fees

Every fee is in US dollars. The introductory meeting, sixty minutes, is $0. A written financial plan, one-off, with three meetings, is $4,800. Ongoing planning is a retainer of $7,200 a year, billed quarterly. Investment management on the first $2 million is 0.80 percent a year. Investment management above $2 million is 0.50 percent a year, with a minimum of $9,600 a year. Hourly project advice is $380 an hour. The firm charges no commissions, no product fees, and no performance fees.

Advisory services are offered for a fee. A household may use one service or several. The investment-management fee is calculated on the assets the firm manages. The planning retainer is for planning, not a substitute label for the management fee. Both can apply when a household wants both. The figures on this page are the figures used in every language the site publishes.

Introductory meeting

Sixty minutes, Tuesday to Thursday, in the office or by video.

$0

Written financial plan

One-off, three meetings. You keep the document.

$4,800

Ongoing planning retainer

Billed quarterly in arrears.

$7,200 / year

Investment management, first $2M

On the first $2 million of assets managed.

0.80% / year

Investment management, above $2M

On assets above $2 million, minimum $9,600 a year.

0.50% / year

Hourly project advice

For a project agreed in advance.

$380 / hour

Two worked examples

These examples show the investment-management fee only. They are arithmetic, not a forecast. A household with $1.5 million invested is entirely inside the first band. The fee is 0.80 percent of $1.5 million, which is $12,000 a year. A household with $3 million invested crosses the band. The first $2 million is charged at 0.80 percent, which is $16,000. The remaining $1 million is charged at 0.50 percent, which is $5,000.

The sum is $21,000 a year. The minimum of $9,600 a year does not change either example, because both calculated fees are already above it. Planning fees are not included in these two figures. A household that also keeps the ongoing planning retainer adds $7,200 a year, billed quarterly. The examples do not show gains or losses. Investing involves risk, including loss of principal.

InvestedCalculationFee a year
$1.5 million0.80% of $1.5 million$12,000
$3 million0.80% of the first $2 million ($16,000) plus 0.50% of the next $1 million ($5,000)$21,000

How billing works

The ongoing planning retainer is billed quarterly in arrears. The household is invoiced for a quarter that has already occurred, not asked to prepay a year. Investment-management fees follow the schedule on this page, 0.80 percent and then 0.50 percent, subject to the yearly minimum of $9,600. The written plan is a one-off fee of $4,800 for three meetings. Hourly work is invoiced at $380 an hour for the project that was agreed.

The introductory meeting is not billed. There is no commission line, no product-fee line, and no performance-fee line on any invoice. Custody is at an independent custodian, and the custodian's own charges, if any, are the custodian's, not a fee invented here. Questions about an invoice go to the office at +1 206 555 0148 or hello@hoshiwealth.example during Monday to Friday, 8:30 to 17:30 Pacific.

Fees

Chapter: 05 — Fees

What the fee does not buy

No commissions · no product fees · no performance fees

A fee buys the work described on the services page. It does not buy a promised return, a tax outcome, or a completed business sale. No strategy assures a profit. The firm will say which adviser leads the work: Naomi Hoshi-Clarke, Tomás Ferreira, Priya Raman, Henrik Aalto, or Grace Mwangi, with Samuel Ortiz-Bell on the papers and Lena Fischer on reporting and compliance. The fee does not rise because a market rose, and it does not include a success charge.

If a household stops, the quarterly billing stops after the quarter already under way, and the written plan the household has paid for remains theirs. Comparing the retainer, the management schedule, and the hourly rate is something the introductory meeting is for. That meeting is free. It is not a credit toward a later fee and not a obligation to continue.

Book an introduction

FEE-ONLY

pages.title: Stories
pages.content:
Four families, four decades.

The reading room at 1418 Western Avenue

Four households show the kinds of questions the firm sits with. Each story is an illustrative composite, with names changed, and none of them reports a result.

Story 01

Chapter: 04 — Story 01

The Moreau-Adeyemi family

Three generations · clients since 2014 · with Naomi Hoshi-Clarke

The Moreau-Adeyemi family has been with Hoshi Wealth Partners since 2014. Three generations plan together. There is a shared house, and there is an education fund for a grandchild. Naomi Hoshi-Clarke is their adviser. The work has been to keep one household's questions from splitting into three unrelated files: who may live in the house, how the education fund is fed, and how the older generation's income sits beside both. A written plan holds those questions in one place.

The investment policy, when they have asked for one, follows the same plan rather than a separate ambition. The firm coordinated with the family's own attorney and tax preparer when estate and giving questions came up. Priya Raman's part of the firm is built for that coordination. This account is an illustrative composite. The names are changed. No balance, no return, and no tax result is stated, because none is claimed.

MOREAU-ADEYEMI

Story 02

Chapter: 04 — Story 02

Walter and June Brennan

Two retiring teachers · with Naomi Hoshi-Clarke

Walter and June Brennan are two retiring teachers. They came to turn pensions and savings into a monthly income. Naomi Hoshi-Clarke works with them. The question they brought is the question her practice is for: what can be spent, in what order, and what has to stay invested so that a later year is not an accident. Their pensions are treated as income the plan can see. Their savings are given a written policy if the firm is asked to manage them.

Nothing in their story depends on a market forecast. The firm does not describe the pensions as ample or thin, and it does not publish the income they drew. A quarterly report, if they are ongoing clients, says whether the spending rule was followed. Two review meetings a year are where the rule is questioned. This account is an illustrative composite. The names are changed. No result is claimed.

BRENNAN

Story 03

Chapter: 04 — Story 03

Rosa Delgado

Furniture workshop owner · with Henrik Aalto

Rosa Delgado owns a furniture workshop. She is preparing to sell it to her employees. Henrik Aalto is her adviser. His practice is business owners who are selling or passing on a firm, and owners whose pay includes equity. Rosa's sale is a plan, not a completed transaction the firm is announcing. The family's spending, the workshop's value to her retirement, and the employees' purchase are three conversations that belong in one document so they are not decided on three different days.

The firm does not broker the sale, does not finance the employees, and does not take a commission from either side. Hourly project advice or a written plan is how this kind of work is billed, at the published fees. No sale price is stated here. This account is an illustrative composite. The name is changed. No result is claimed.

DELGADO

Story 04

Chapter: 04 — Story 04

Amir and Hana Saleh

Young parents · with Grace Mwangi

Amir and Hana Saleh are young parents writing their first plan. Grace Mwangi, associate adviser, works with them. A first plan is the firm's $4,800 engagement: three meetings and a document the household keeps. They are not asked to become investment-management clients in order to finish it. The plan names what the money is for, what is owed, and what a later year might need. Papers stay face-down until the household is ready to put them in the document.

Tomás Ferreira's investment policy is available if they later ask the firm to invest. It is not a requirement of the first plan. The firm does not show a sample portfolio for them and does not invent a savings rate. This account is an illustrative composite. The names are changed. No result is claimed. Young families are the work Grace is here to do.

SALEH

A note on these four stories

These four accounts are illustrative composites. Names are changed. They are not case studies with outcomes, and they are not testimonials. The Moreau-Adeyemi family shows three generations, a shared house, and a grandchild's education fund, with Naomi Hoshi-Clarke, since 2014. Walter and June Brennan show two retiring teachers arranging pensions and savings as monthly income, also with Naomi. Rosa Delgado shows an owner preparing to sell a furniture workshop to her employees, with Henrik Aalto.

Amir and Hana Saleh show young parents writing a first plan, with Grace Mwangi. No story states a return, a balance, a sale price, or a tax saving. About 140 households work with the firm. These four are here so a reader can see the kinds of questions the seven people sit with. They are not a promise that a new household's facts will look the same.

Stage 01

Introductory meeting

60 min

The introductory meeting is sixty minutes. It costs $0. It is offered on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday, in the Seattle office or by video. Thursday meetings can run until 19:00 by appointment. The office is at 1418 Western Avenue, Suite 600, Seattle, WA 98101. There is no pitch and no packet of products, because the firm does not sell products. The hour is for the household to say what the money is for, and for the adviser to say whether the firm does that work.

Naomi Hoshi-Clarke, Tomás Ferreira, Priya Raman, Henrik Aalto, or Grace Mwangi may host, depending on the question. You do not receive a plan in the hour. You leave knowing the fee, the next stage, and whether you want it. Booking is by email at hello@hoshiwealth.example or by phone at +1 206 555 0148.

Stage 02

Discovery

2 weeks

Discovery takes about two weeks. Documents are gathered, and there is one working session. Samuel Ortiz-Bell coordinates the paperwork, the transfers if any are later required, and the meeting notes. The household brings the papers that show what it already has: accounts, pensions, debts, a will or the absence of one, and any question it wants written down. Nothing must be moved during these two weeks. The independent custodian is not involved until the household decides the firm should manage money.

The working session is where gaps show up. A missing statement is better found here than inside a finished plan. Discovery is part of preparing the written plan. It is not a separate fee. The $0 introductory meeting has already happened, and the plan fee, if the household proceeds, is the $4,800 fee for three meetings.

Stage 03

Written plan

6 weeks

The written plan is presented within six weeks of the first meeting. It is the document from the $4,800 engagement, shaped across three meetings, of which the introductory meeting is the first conversation and not a billed hour. The plan says what the household is trying to do, what resources it has named, and what decision comes next. If investment management is part of the request, Tomás Ferreira's policy is written before funds are chosen.

If the question is retirement income, the spending rule is in the plan. If the question is a business sale or an estate, Henrik or Priya writes the coordination points, not a legal document. The household keeps the plan. Presentation is a meeting, not a slideshow of returns. The firm will not attach a performance target to the back page.

Stage 04

Ongoing

Quarterly

Ongoing work is for households that want the firm to stay. The planning retainer is $7,200 a year, billed quarterly in arrears. Investment management, if chosen, is 0.80 percent a year on the first $2 million and 0.50 percent a year above that, minimum $9,600 a year. The ongoing service includes a quarterly report, two review meetings a year, and a written investment policy updated yearly. Lena Fischer oversees reporting and the disclosures.

Samuel keeps notes. The adviser does not change unless the household's question changes. A household can stop. The quarterly bill covers the quarter in arrears, and it does not include a leaving fee, a commission, or a performance calculation. The same four stages apply whether the household met in the office or on video. Weekend meetings are not held. The office is closed on US public holidays.

pages.title: Disclosures
pages.content:
Disclosures

Advisory services are offered for a fee. Investing involves risk, including loss of principal, and no strategy assures a profit.

Fee-only statement

Hoshi Wealth Partners offers advisory services for a fee. The firm is fee-only. It was founded in 2009. Clients pay the fees published on this site, in US dollars: $0 for the introductory meeting, $4,800 for a written financial plan, $7,200 a year for the ongoing planning retainer, 0.80 percent a year on the first $2 million of assets managed, 0.50 percent a year above $2 million with a minimum of $9,600 a year, and $380 an hour for project advice.

The firm does not receive commissions. It does not receive product fees. It does not receive performance fees. Those absences are the conflicts the firm has chosen not to create. Investing involves risk, including loss of principal. No strategy assures a profit. Nothing on this site is a promise of a result. The seven people named here are the people who do the work.

Conflicts

A fee-only firm still has conflicts, and they should be named in ordinary language. The firm is paid more when a household continues an ongoing retainer, and more when more assets are managed, because the management fee is a percentage, subject to the published minimum. That is a reason for a household to read the quarterly report and to use the two review meetings a year. It is not hidden. The firm is not paid more for choosing one index fund over another, and it is not paid by a product sponsor.

It does not charge more in a strong market through a performance fee. Hourly work is a conflict of a different shape: more hours cost more. The scope of an hourly project is agreed before the hours run. The firm does not claim that fee-only removes judgment. It claims that the judgment is not paid for by a third party.

Custody

The firm does not take custody of client assets. Investments managed by the firm are held at an independent custodian. The custodian is not named on this site and is not a brand the firm advertises. Clients receive the custodian's own statements as well as the firm's quarterly report. Lena Fischer's operations work includes reconciling the firm's reporting to custody records. Samuel Ortiz-Bell handles transfer paperwork when a household decides to move assets.

A transfer happens only after the household has asked for it. Discovery, the two weeks after an introductory meeting, does not itself move money. The custodian's charges, if the custodian charges any, are not fees of Hoshi Wealth Partners and are not restated here as if they were. Questions about where assets are held are answered in the meeting and in the written plan.

Privacy

The firm uses household information to prepare the plan, to report, to bill, and to meet its compliance duties. Meeting notes, transfer papers, and the documents gathered in discovery stay with the people who need them for that work: the adviser, Samuel Ortiz-Bell, and Lena Fischer. The firm does not publish client lists. The four families on the stories page are illustrative composites with names changed. They are not a disclosure of real accounts.

The site does not ask for a password, an account number, or a social-security number. Do not send those by email. The address hello@hoshiwealth.example is for booking and for questions. The phone +1 206 555 0148 reaches the office Monday to Friday, 8:30 to 17:30 Pacific. Information is kept for the household it belongs to. It is not a marketing list.

posts.title: The policy is written before the funds are chosen
posts.excerpt: A letter from the desk on why Hoshi Wealth Partners writes the investment policy first and reports against that policy every quarter.
posts.content:
A household can feel the pressure to do something with money the moment it is discussed. A fund is named. A headline is quoted. Someone asks whether this is a good week to begin. At Hoshi Wealth Partners the order runs the other way. Tomás Ferreira, our chief investment officer, writes the investment policy before any fund is chosen. The policy says what the money is for, how long it has to work, and what mix the household can keep. Only then do we look for low-cost index funds that match what was written. The sequence is the practice, not a preface we skip when the calendar is loud.

We started the firm in 2009 as a fee-only practice, and the policy is one reason that structure still matters. Naomi Hoshi-Clarke founded Hoshi Wealth Partners so the household in the room would be the party that pays. We do not receive commissions, product fees, or performance fees. If a fund is in a portfolio, it is there because the policy called for that kind of holding, not because a sponsor paid us to prefer it. Custody sits with an independent custodian we do not advertise. Our fee for management, when a household asks for it, is 0.80 percent a year on the first $2 million and 0.50 percent a year above that, with a minimum of $9,600 a year. Those are the dollars. They are not a forecast.

Fewer moves follow from the same page. Rebalancing is a rule written in advance. When the mix drifts past what the policy allows, we bring it back. When it has not drifted, we leave it. A quiet quarter is not a quarter in which we failed to pay attention. It is often a quarter in which the rule said to wait. We update the written policy yearly, and we also change it when a household's life changes: a retirement, a sale of a firm, a grandchild's education, the first plan a young family has ever written. We do not change it because a month was noisy.

The quarterly report is where this becomes visible. Ongoing clients receive a report in plain words. It states the policy, what the rule required, and what the household paid. Two review meetings a year are the time to argue with that report. Samuel Ortiz-Bell keeps the notes. Lena Fischer watches the reporting against the custodian's records. The adviser across the table may be Naomi, Tomás, Priya Raman, Henrik Aalto, or Grace Mwangi, depending on whose work the household came for. The standard does not change with the name. If a sentence in the report only makes sense to the person who drafted it, it is rewritten before it goes out.

This is also why we will not use a letter like this one to predict a market. A letter can remind you of a rule. It cannot see your pensions, your workshop, your shared house, or your first plan. Walter and June Brennan's question, how two retiring teachers turn pensions and savings into monthly income, is not answered by a commentary. Rosa Delgado's question, how to prepare a sale of her furniture workshop to her employees, is not answered by one either. The Moreau-Adeyemi family, clients since 2014, and Amir and Hana Saleh, writing their first plan, are in the same position. Those stories are composites. The names are changed. We cite them to show the kind of work, and we stop before any result.

If you want to know whether the sequence fits your own facts, the introductory meeting is sixty minutes, it costs nothing, and it is not a pitch. We hold it on Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday, at 1418 Western Avenue, Suite 600, Seattle, or by video. You can write to hello@hoshiwealth.example or call +1 206 555 0148. Office hours are Monday to Friday, 8:30 to 17:30 Pacific. Come with the question. You do not need a decision, and you do not need to move a single account to have the conversation.

posts.title: What a quarterly report is for.
posts.excerpt: A quarterly report says what the firm did, what it cost, and what is unchanged. It carries no forecast.
posts.content:
A quarterly report has three jobs. It says what the firm did in the last three months, what that cost, and what is unchanged. That is all.

Most quarters the honest answer to the first question is very little: a rebalance because a rule said so, perhaps a withdrawal for the household's monthly income. The cost is shown in dollars, not only as a percentage, so a household can see exactly what the invoice bought.

The report has no forecast and no market commentary written to sound clever. If the written investment policy is working, the report should be short and a little dull. That is the point.

posts.title: Why the firm stays small.
posts.excerpt: Seven people, one table and about one hundred forty households: why Hoshi Wealth Partners has kept the firm small on purpose.
posts.content:
Hoshi Wealth Partners has seven people and about one hundred forty households. That ratio is a decision, not an accident. Naomi Hoshi-Clarke opened the firm in 2009 so that a family could sit with the same adviser year after year.

A small firm can keep its promises to individual households. The person who wrote your plan still answers the phone, and the partners read every quarterly report before it is sent. When a household's life changes, the people who need to know are in the same room.

If the firm ever grows, it will be by adding a table, not by stretching one. For now, seven people share one reading room on Western Avenue, and that is enough.
